title: A Detroit beer program and Phil Wall's quick arrangements
summary: A sponsor told him not to educate listeners with divided strings, and he would not copy Phil Wall's fast formula arrangements.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Now, this is a case where I didn't have exact instructions, but I think what they figured is I should have known better, because I'd worked on the Lucky Strike before. I had another experience with a guy who used -- who used to do a beer program out in Detroit. He used to go out there and do
this show with the Detroit Symphony, and it was a nice -- it was a nice job.

They paid well for the arrangements, you know, and the band was big. That was the way you'd tell if it's a good job or not. If the band was big, you got paid so much a page and for so many instruments.

And so I made an arrangement one time, and I had a couple of little things in there that I had done and that I carried over, let's say, from the dance business, which I was doing all the time, because that was my -- that was my bag.

So I did it, did it with strings, and I thought, 'Well, a little unusual to do this.' And he called me in one time after it, and he says, 'You know, that's nice,' he says. 'Strings are nice when you divide them and get a lot of harmony out of them, but,' he said, 'we're not trying to educate them.'

He didn't want me to do that anymore. So he gave me a couple of Phil Walls arrangements to look over. And, you know, Phil was a piano player on Kostelanetz' show and on this guy's show, and he used to make -- I heard one time that he had made 18 arrangements in one week.
Let's say at 50 bucks in those days --

he'd probably get paid by the page, but an average fee of 50 bucks, that's a lot of money. Somebody told me that he never spent any of his arranging money. He only spent what he had to live on playing the job.

Well, I looked at it, you know. There isn't a nicer effect than all the strings playing in unison, you know, particularly in the low register, and I thought, My God, a guy could do this going home in the subway after he got the assignment.
But I couldn't bring myself around to that. So actually with few exceptions I was an unsuccessful radio orchestrator. I knew my business --
But it wasn't what you were --
-- but -- as far as orchestration was concerned -- but as far as making money was concerned, I just couldn't get around to that, you know, force it out.
